name: Japanese: Hiragana
author: Recurse
subject: languages
description: Read all 46 basic hiragana, voicing marks, small kana, long vowels and your first simple sentences.

lesson.intro: Japanese is written with three scripts, and hiragana is where every learner starts. Each character is a whole syllable, so once you know the 46 basic characters and two small marks, you can sound out any word written in hiragana.
objectives: Explain how hiragana, katakana and kanji share the work
Read all 46 basic hiragana, including shi, chi, tsu and fu
Read voiced sounds with dakuten and handakuten, and syllables with small ゃ, ゅ, ょ
Hear and read double consonants and long vowels
Read simple sentences built with は, を, の, です and か

sections.title: Three scripts and the five vowels
sections.key: Japanese mixes three scripts: hiragana for native words and grammar, katakana for loanwords, kanji for meaning. Each hiragana character is a whole syllable.
sections.body:
A normal Japanese sentence mixes three scripts:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Hiragana and katakana are **syllabaries**: each character stands for a whole sound, usually a consonant plus a vowel, not a single letter. This pack spells sounds in **Hepburn romanization**, the system English speakers see most often.

Everything starts with the five vowels, always in this order:

[[visual 3]]

They are short and pure: roughly a as in father, i as in ski, u as in food (with relaxed lips), e as in pet, o as in old without the glide.

Hiragana also unlocks kanji you have not learned yet: learner books print **furigana**, tiny hiragana beside a kanji to show how it is read.

visual.title: Three scripts
rows: Native words and grammar: particles, verb endings. Young children's books are almost all hiragana

visual.title: 私はコーヒーを飲みます。 (watashi wa kōhī o nomimasu: I drink coffee.)

sections.pitfall: Thinking you must learn kanji before you can read anything. Hiragana alone covers particles, verb endings, children's books and the furigana printed beside kanji.

check.question: Which hiragana is read 'o'?
check.explanation: お is o. It looks a little like あ (a), so compare the right side: お has a separate short stroke at the top right.

sections.title: The k, s, t and n rows
sections.key: Each row puts a consonant before the five vowels in a, i, u, e, o order, but three readings break the pattern: し shi, ち chi and つ tsu.
sections.body:
Each new row puts a consonant in front of the five vowels, in the same a, i, u, e, o order. Most readings are what you would expect, but three break the pattern: し is shi (not si), ち is chi (not ti) and つ is tsu (not tu).

[[visual]]

Look-alikes to watch:

- さ (sa) and ち (chi) are close to mirror images.
- き (ki) is さ (sa) with one extra horizontal stroke.
- ぬ (nu) ends in a small loop; め (me, next section) does not.

Practice words: あき aki (autumn), すし sushi, ねこ neko (cat), いぬ inu (dog), たかい takai (tall, expensive).

Write with the standard stroke order, generally top to bottom and left to right. Pictures help the shapes stick: ね is a cat (neko) with a curled tail, and き looks a little like a key.

visual.title: The k, s, t and n rows
visual.caption: Highlighted: the readings that break the pattern.

sections.tip: Say each row aloud in order (ka, ki, ku, ke, ko); the fixed vowel order makes rows easy to rebuild from memory.
sections.pitfall: Romanizing し as si, ち as ti and つ as tu. In Hepburn they are shi, chi and tsu, which match how they actually sound.

check.question: Which hiragana is read 'nu'?
check.explanation: ぬ is nu. ね is ne, の is no and な is na; ぬ and ね both end in a loop, so look at the left side: ね has a straight vertical stroke.

sections.title: The h, m, y, r and w rows, and ん
sections.key: The h, m, y, r and w rows and ん complete the 46 basic hiragana; ふ is read fu, を is read o, and ん is the only lone consonant.
sections.body:
The remaining rows complete the set:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

- **ふ** is fu, a soft f made by blowing between the lips.
- The Japanese **r** is a light tap of the tongue, between an English r, l and d.
- **を** is pronounced o and used almost only as the object particle, so Hepburn writes it o (charts often show wo).
- **ん** is the only character that is a consonant on its own: n, as in ほん hon (book). Before p, b and m it sounds closer to m.

As **particles**, は is read wa when it marks the topic (これは kore wa) and へ is read e when it means toward.

Look-alikes: れ (re), わ (wa) and ね (ne) share a left stroke and differ on the right; る (ru) ends in a loop, ろ (ro) does not.

visual.title: The h, m and r rows
The y and w rows, and ん

sections.pitfall: Mixing up れ, わ and ね, or る and ろ. Check the right side of the character and whether the last stroke ends in a loop.

check.question: Which hiragana is read 'mu'?
check.explanation: む is mu. す (su) has a similar loop but no stroke on the right, and ぬ is nu from the n row.

sections.title: Dakuten and handakuten
sections.key: Two small marks make new sounds from old shapes: dakuten (゛) turns k, s, t and h into g, z, d and b, and handakuten (゜) turns h into p.
sections.body:
Two small marks turn basic characters into new sounds, so there are no new shapes to learn. The **dakuten** (゛, two short strokes at the top right) voices the consonant. The **handakuten** (゜, a small circle) appears only on the h row and turns h into p.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

ぢ and づ are rare; じ and ず are normally used instead.

[[visual 3]]

Practice words: かぎ kagi (key), みず mizu (water), でんわ denwa (telephone), ぶた buta (pig), ぴかぴか pikapika (shiny).

visual.title: What the marks do
rows: ち → ぢ ji, つ → づ zu

visual.title: With dakuten: g, z and d
b with dakuten, p with handakuten

sections.pitfall: Putting the small circle on other rows. Handakuten (゜) only goes on the h row to make p sounds; every other voiced sound uses the two-stroke dakuten.

check.question: Which hiragana is read 'pi'?
check.explanation: ぴ is pi: ひ (hi) plus the small circle. び has the two-stroke dakuten instead, so it is bi.

sections.title: Small ゃ ゅ ょ and first words
sections.key: A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ merges with the i-column character before it into one syllable, so きょ is kyo but きよ, with a full-size よ, is ki-yo.
sections.body:
A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ after a consonant character from the i column (き, し, ち, に, ひ, み, り, and marked forms such as ぎ, じ, び, ぴ) merges with it into one syllable: き ki + small ゃ = きゃ kya.

[[visual]]

Size matters: きょ (kyo) is one beat, but きよ with a full-size よ is two (ki-yo). A small っ works differently: it doubles the next consonant, as in きって kitte (postage stamp).

Long vowels are written with an extra vowel character. An o followed by う is usually a long o, which Hepburn marks with a macron: とうきょう is Tōkyō. Typing often uses ou or just o.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: First words
rows: hello (the final は is read wa)
ありがとうございます

sections.pitfall: Reading a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ as a full syllable. きょ is one beat, kyo; only a full-size よ gives ki-yo.

check.question: How is しょ read?
check.explanation: The small ょ merges with し into the single syllable sho. Shiyo would be the reading of しよ with a full-size よ.

sections.title: Double consonants and long vowels
sections.key: Each kana, plus ん and the small っ, is one beat, so length changes meaning: おばさん (aunt) has four beats and おばあさん (grandmother) five.
sections.body:
Japanese is timed in beats called **morae**: each full-size kana, plus ん and the small っ, takes about the same time. So length changes meaning, and careful listening pays off.

A **small っ** (small tsu) adds a one-beat pause and doubles the next consonant: きて kite (come) versus きって kitte (postage stamp, ki-t-te). Hepburn doubles the consonant, as in ざっし zasshi (magazine) and いっぱい ippai (full); before ch it writes t: まっちゃ matcha.

**Long vowels** last two beats instead of one:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Hepburn marks long vowels with a macron (ā, ī, ū, ē, ō), but signs and typing often drop it: Tokyo, Osaka. Katakana marks them with a dash: コーヒー kōhī.

visual.title: Spelling long vowels
rows: えい (a few words: ええ)
せんせい sensei (teacher), said sen-sē; おねえさん onēsan (older sister)
おう (a few words: おお)
とうきょう Tōkyō, ありがとう arigatō; おおきい ōkii (big), とお tō (ten)

sections.pitfall: Rushing long vowels and double consonants. おばあさん has five beats and おばさん has four; give every kana, long vowel and small っ its full beat.

check.question: How is ざっし (magazine) read in Hepburn romanization?
check.explanation: The small っ doubles the next consonant, and Hepburn writes the doubled sh as ssh: zasshi. Zatsushi reads the small っ as a full-size つ, and zashi drops the pause entirely.

sections.title: First sentences: は, を, の, です and か
sections.key: Particles do the grammar: は (wa) marks the topic, を (o) the object, の links nouns, です ends a polite statement and か makes it a question.
sections.body:
With hiragana alone you can read simple sentences, because grammar words are always written in hiragana.

[[visual]]

The **verb comes last**: topic or subject, then object, then verb, so "I eat sushi" is literally "I sushi eat". Subjects are often left out when clear: すしを たべます alone means I eat sushi.

[[visual 2]]

Beginner texts put spaces between phrases, but normal Japanese uses none, which is one reason kanji help: they show where content words begin. The period is 。 and the comma is 、.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Particles and endings
rows: Marks the topic, what the sentence is about
わたしは がくせいです watashi wa gakusei desu: I am a student
Marks the direct object, the thing acted on
すしを たべます sushi o tabemasu: I eat sushi
Links two nouns, a bit like 's
わたしの ほん watashi no hon: my book; にほんの くるま: a Japanese car
Ends a polite statement, like "is" or "am". The u is almost silent: "dess"
がくせいです: (I) am a student
At the end, turns a statement into a question; word order stays the same
これは ほんですか kore wa hon desu ka: Is this a book?

visual.title: わたしは すしを たべます。

messages.label: これは なんですか。
messages.detail: kore wa nan desu ka: What is this?

messages.label: それは わたしの かさです。
messages.detail: sore wa watashi no kasa desu: That is my umbrella.

sections.pitfall: Reading は and を with their usual sounds inside a sentence. As particles they are wa and o: わたしは is watashi wa, not watashi ha.

check.question: What does の do in わたしの ほん?
choices: It marks the topic of the sentence
It links the two nouns: my book
It turns the phrase into a question
It marks the object of a verb
check.explanation: の connects two nouns, with the first describing or owning the second: わたしの ほん is my book. The topic marker is は, the object marker is を, and か makes a question.

keyTerms.definition: The rounded Japanese syllabary used for native words, particles and verb endings; 46 basic characters.
The angular syllabary used mainly for foreign loanwords and names, such as コーヒー (kōhī, coffee).
Characters borrowed from Chinese that carry meaning, such as 山 (yama, mountain).
The most widely used way to write Japanese in Latin letters; it spells し shi, ち chi, つ tsu and ふ fu.
The two-stroke mark ゛ that voices a consonant: か ka → が ga, は ha → ば ba.
The small circle ゜ added to the h row to make p sounds: は ha → ぱ pa.
A combined syllable written with a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ, such as きょ kyo or しゃ sha.
One beat of Japanese timing; each full-size kana, ん and the small っ each take one beat.
A small tsu that adds a pause and doubles the next consonant: きって kitte (stamp).
Small hiragana printed above or beside kanji to show how they are read.
A short grammar word written in hiragana after a noun to show its role, such as は (topic), を (object) and の (possession).

summary: Hiragana for native words and grammar, katakana for loanwords, kanji for meaning.
The 46 basic hiragana are the vowels plus consonant rows; watch shi, chi, tsu and fu.
Dakuten (゛) voices a consonant (か ka → が ga); handakuten (゜) makes p (ぱ pa).
Small ゃ, ゅ, ょ merge (きょ kyo); small っ doubles the next consonant (きって kitte).
Each kana is one beat: おばさん is aunt, おばあさん grandmother.
As particles は, へ and を are read wa, e and o: これは ほんですか.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain how hiragana, katakana and kanji share the work in a Japanese sentence, and how dakuten and the small ゃ, ゅ, ょ let you read new sounds without learning new characters.

questions.question: Which script is mainly used to write foreign loanwords, such as words borrowed from English?
questions.explanation: Katakana is the script for most loanwords and foreign names, like コーヒー (kōhī, coffee). Hiragana, the tempting answer, is used for native words and grammar.

questions.question: What are the three Japanese scripts, and what is each mainly used for?
questions.answer: Hiragana for native words and grammar (particles, verb endings), katakana for foreign loanwords and names, and kanji, Chinese-derived characters that carry the meaning of most content words.
questions.explanation: Most sentences mix all three. In 私はコーヒーを飲みます (I drink coffee), 私 and 飲 are kanji, コーヒー is katakana, and は, を and みます are hiragana.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: あおい (blue)
questions.explanation: あ is a, お is o and い is i, so あおい is aoi. Each vowel is pronounced separately: a-o-i.

questions.question: Read this hiragana in Hepburn romanization: し
questions.explanation: し is shi, one of the irregular readings in the s row (sa, shi, su, se, so). Some other systems write si, but Hepburn uses shi because it matches the sound.

questions.question: Read this hiragana in Hepburn romanization: つ
questions.explanation: つ is tsu, not tu. The t row goes ta, chi, tsu, te, to.

questions.question: Which hiragana is read 'chi'?
questions.explanation: ち is chi. It is close to a mirror image of さ (sa), which is the usual mix-up; き is ki and ら is ra.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: さかな (fish)
questions.explanation: さ sa + か ka + な na gives sakana.
questions.concept: reading the k, s, t, n rows

questions.question: Read this hiragana in Hepburn romanization: ふ
questions.explanation: ふ is fu, the irregular member of the h row (ha, hi, fu, he, ho). The sound is a soft f made with both lips, which is why Hepburn does not write hu.

questions.question: Which hiragana is read 're'?
questions.explanation: れ is re. わ (wa) and ね (ne) share the same left stroke, so check the right side: れ ends in a flick outward, わ in a rounded curve and ね in a small loop. る is ru.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: みかん (mandarin orange)
questions.explanation: み mi + か ka + ん n gives mikan. ん is the only hiragana that is a consonant on its own.

questions.question: Which three hiragana are read differently when they are used as particles?
questions.answer: は is read wa (topic marker), へ is read e (direction, toward) and を is read o (object marker).
questions.explanation: In ordinary words they keep their normal sounds, as in はな hana (flower) and へや heya (room). The particle readings are old spellings that Japanese has kept.

questions.question: Read this hiragana in Hepburn romanization: じ
questions.explanation: Adding dakuten to し (shi) gives じ, read ji. It is not zi, in the same way that し is not si.

questions.question: Adding dakuten (゛) to は (ha) gives which sound?
questions.explanation: The dakuten turns the h row into b, so ば is ba. Pa comes from the small circle, the handakuten (ぱ), not from dakuten.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: えんぴつ (pencil)
questions.explanation: え e + ん n + ぴ pi + つ tsu gives enpitsu. Because ん sounds like m before p, the older Hepburn spelling empitsu is also correct.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: でんしゃ (train)
questions.explanation: で de + ん n + しゃ sha gives densha. The small ゃ merges with し into the single syllable sha; reading it as den-shi-ya is the common mistake.

questions.question: What is the difference between きよ and きょ?
choices: きよ is two syllables (ki-yo); きょ is one (kyo)
They are two spellings of the same sound
きよ is one syllable (kyo); きょ is two (ki-yo)
きよ is katakana; きょ is hiragana
questions.explanation: A full-size よ is its own syllable, so きよ is ki-yo. A small ょ merges with the character before it, so きょ is the single syllable kyo.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: こんにちは (hello)
questions.explanation: こ ko + ん n + に ni + ち chi + は wa. The last character is は, but it is read wa because the greeting began as a phrase ending in the topic particle. Konnichiha is the common misreading.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: ありがとう (thank you)
questions.explanation: あ a + り ri + が ga + とう tō. The final とう is a long o, written ō in Hepburn; arigatou and arigato are common keyboard spellings. Add ございます (gozaimasu) to be more polite.

questions.question: Match each look-alike hiragana to its reading.
questions.explanation: ね, れ and わ share a left stroke and differ on the right: a loop for ne, an outward flick for re, a rounded curve for wa. ぬ has a loop at the end and め does not; る ends in a loop, unlike ろ.

questions.question: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Reading each word aloud first helps: neko, inu, mizu, hon, kasa and densha. Pairing the sound with its meaning practices both the kana and your first vocabulary.

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: きって (postage stamp)
questions.explanation: The small っ doubles the next consonant: き ki + っ + て te gives kitte, three beats. Without the small っ, きて is kite (come).

questions.question: Read this word in Hepburn romanization: おばあさん (grandmother)
questions.explanation: あ after ば lengthens the a: o-ba-a-sa-n, written obāsan. Shortening it to obasan gives おばさん, which means aunt.

questions.question: What is the difference between おばさん and おばあさん?
choices: They are two spellings of the word for grandmother
おばあさん is the plural of おばさん
おばさん (obasan) means aunt; おばあさん (obāsan), with a long a, means grandmother
おばさん is polite and おばあさん is casual
questions.explanation: Vowel length is part of the word in Japanese. The extra あ adds a beat and turns aunt into grandmother, just as ゆき (snow) becomes ゆうき (courage).

questions.question: Read this sentence in Hepburn romanization: わたしは がくせいです (I am a student.)
questions.explanation: は is the topic particle here, so it is read wa, not ha. がくせい is gakusei (the final い lengthens the e), and です is desu.

questions.question: Which phrase means "my book"?
questions.explanation: の links two nouns with the owner first: わたしの ほん, my book. ほんの わたし reverses it (the book's me), and は and を mark the topic and the object instead.

questions.question: Select every word that contains a long vowel.
questions.explanation: とうきょう has two long o sounds (Tōkyō), せんせい ends in a long e written with い (sensē), おおきい starts with a long o (ōkii), and くうき has a long u (kūki). ゆき and ねこ have only short vowels.

questions.question: Put the parts in order to say "I eat sushi."
questions.explanation: Japanese puts the verb last: topic (わたしは), then object (すしを), then verb (たべます). The particles show each word's role, so the verb-final order is what matters most.

questions.question: Read this question in Hepburn romanization: これは なんですか (What is this?)
questions.explanation: これ kore + は wa (topic particle) + なん nan (what) + です desu + か ka (question marker). Reading は as ha is the common slip.

questions.question: What are furigana?
choices: The dash that marks long vowels in katakana
Small hiragana printed beside kanji to show how they are read
The kanji used to write verb endings
questions.explanation: Furigana are reading aids printed above or beside kanji, common in children's books and learner materials. The long-vowel dash belongs to katakana, verb endings are written in hiragana, and ゛ is the dakuten.
